title: Four feelings words in two languages: the mirror game for happy, sad, tired, scared
description: Stand in front of any mirror and make faces together: happy, sad, tired, scared. Name each face in the language you are building, as a game, while nobody is actually upset.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: Four feelings words in two languages: the mirror game for happy, sad, tired, scared
body:
Feelings words are the ones children reach for when everything is running high, which is the worst moment to learn them. Practising them as a game, in front of a mirror, while nobody is upset, is a gentler way to meet them.

Any mirror works: the bathroom one, a hallway mirror, a wardrobe door. Stand side by side so you can both see your faces.

Start with four feelings: happy, sad, tired, scared. In Spanish: feliz, triste, cansado or cansada, asustado or asustada. The -o or -a ending follows the person it describes; feliz and triste stay the same for everyone.

Round one: you make a face, and your child names it in the language you are building. If you are building Spanish: you droop your shoulders and yawn, and they say "¡cansado!" (or "¡cansada!", depending on who is making the face). If you are building English: you pull a sad face, and they say "sad!".

Round two: swap. Your child makes a face and you guess — sometimes wrongly, on purpose, so they can correct you: "¿Estás feliz?" "¡No, triste!" / "Are you happy?" "No, sad!".

Round three: add a reason. "Estoy feliz porque…" / "I'm happy because…". Let your child finish the sentence in whichever language comes out. The reason is the part that turns a single word into a conversation.

Keep the game short, three or four minutes, and stop while you are both still laughing.

The words get their real use later in the day. When your child is actually tired or sad, offer the word quietly in the language you are building — "¿Estás cansado?" or "are you tired?" — and let them nod or answer. Do not turn a hard moment into practice; just make the word available.

After a week, add two more: surprised and calm — sorprendido or sorprendida, tranquilo or tranquila. Same game, same mirror.

semantic_review: English body; Spanish adjectives with gender agreement explained plainly (cansado/cansada, asustado/asustada; feliz and triste unchanged). Word for angry left out because it differs between Spain and Latin America. Scripts in both directions for naming, guessing and giving a reason.
